title: What is Borderline Personality Disorder?
subtitle: A speech I gave in September, 2016.
text:
This is a daily healthcare newsletter written by Owen Muir, M.D. The following is adapted from a speech I gave in 2016.

46,000 Americans killed themselves this year. Close to 500,000 visited an ER for "self-inflicted harm," which includes attempts at suicide.

Subscribe now

Shakespeare did a better job of understanding that humans have personalities, and sometimes they aren't working as well as they should, which can lead people to complete suicide. Ophelia, Lady Macbeth, Timon of Athens, almost everyone other than Julius Caesar except Julius Caesar, the list goes on. I'm a psychiatrist as part of a long story that includes my grandfather's life ending in 1939 at the end of a noose in his basement. I have another family member who miraculously didn't die when the liver transplant she was denied to treat her liver failure after an overdose attempt didn't end up being required. We don't know for sure what my family members, or any other people who died from suicide, were suffering from. Or if they had any mental illness at all. Most do, however. And borderline personality disorder, or "BPD," noticed or not, is a major contributor to these deaths. Deaths none of us needed.

Yes, I took this picture. © Owen Muir, 2023.

We are here tonight to light the way forward for people who are struggling with suicide and the people whose lives are affected by that struggle. Suicide is the final common pathway of a variety of ills. However, unlike a heart attack, stroke, or other causes of death, the Medical Examiner's Office will not find the cause of anyone's suicide. Furthermore, unlike most causes of death, suicide ends the lives of many young people. It is the third leading cause of death of young people in America. In the wake of someone's death by their own hand, a lingering question among survivors is, "Why"?

It turns out the answer to that question is extremely difficult to answer for a person or a population. If rhinovirus were killing as many people a year as suicide, many of whom were young and unrecognized as having an illness, we'd be hearing about it. It would be a national priority if your friend's heart attack made you more likely to die from one.

Comparisons can be useful to frame our understanding: This neglect and silence is not true for breast cancer. People are wearing ribbons. People wear survivor shirts. People tell their stories, and families and friends gather around those afflicted. Breast cancer kills fewer people than annually than suicide in the US. Fewer people have nonfatal than are evaluated in a hospital for self-inflicted harm. And yet every day is breast cancer awareness day.

And by the way, many people who attempt or complete suicide aren't counted in those statistics. They don't hit a hospital emergency room or get counted. They wake up after their overdose in a hotel room. They get up from the train tracks before the train arrives. They slowly walk down the stairs from the roof. We are here to shine some light on one of the often unrecognized contributors to this epidemic of bone-deep misery and generational trauma that is suicide. Two psychiatric illnesses have suicidal thoughts mentioned in our diagnostic manual, the DSM-5.

One is depression. Most of us can wrap our heads around that. "Major depressive disorder" sounds like feeling bad. Most people have felt bad. We get that concept. The other illness many people haven't heard of, and is misunderstood by many, many more. That includes therapists and doctors, nurses, and other medical professionals. It's got a name. It's a problematic name, named long ago for reasons that made sense in that era. But we are stuck with it for the time being.

It's called “Borderline Personality Disorder."

"What the hell is that supposed to mean?" Do you say?

Exactly. It's an illness that was named and recognized within our lifetimes, heck, the guys who named it and defined it are still working as a psychiatrist. Otto Kernberg, He's here in NYC. John Gunderson is still teaching people around the country, to name just two. So how can we understand it if we haven't lived it? I'll give it a shot as a doctor and family member.

Imagine you had 3rd degree burns all over your body, and no one could see them. You look the same. But any connection with someone else, rejection, even the thought of it, and you are in pain. It's not obvious to others why you look so hurt-- remember, no one can see the burns. So you get people telling you to "just" calm down. But you can't. And "just" makes it sound so easy to do? Why can't I "just" do it? I must be a broken person. Meanwhile, the people suffering this way have some coping mechanisms...and welcome back suicide. One is thoughts of suicide, self-injury, or even suicide attempts.

Depression is an episodic Illness. Borderline Personality Disorder is less, though it waxes and wanes. So instead of feeling suicidal in the dark night of the soul, that can be every day. It has other features: chronic emptiness, feeling dissociated and out of your body, anger that is out of control, impulsivity, interpersonal chaos, unstable mood, risky choices around drugs, sex, food, driving, and even psychotic symptoms can happen--hallucinations, paranoia.

Sounds miserable and confusing? I agree. The numbers on how lethal this illness is are often misstated. People say 10% die by suicide. I don't think that's the most accurate estimate. The largest study following BPD almost 20 years found a number under 5%. That is still awful.

On top of that, there is a horrible stigma, and psychiatrists and other people in health care are at fault here. We don't understand that BPD naturally has a good prognosis. We tend to think it makes you a difficult "borderline" forever and to avoid other people thinking the same stigmatizing things we are, doctors don't make the diagnosis. It's depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder—anything but BPD.

In young people, it's even been worse. I've had senior administrators Sit me down and tell me, "You will never make a personality disorder diagnosis in a child or adolescent again. It shouldn't even be considered." What would I think if I had BPD hearing that? Or if I were in recovery like so many of my colleagues?

The truth about suicide, as I understand it, it that it is a plague upon the house of humanity and has been with us for a very long time. And we don't “know” systematically how to stop it. But I know with certainty we are missing the boat on a great many people by diagnosing every hard time for another human struggling with misery and sadness, "major depressive disorder," or worse yet, "bipolar disorder," if they are "moody.”

To the best of our knowledge, we can't medicate away the suffering and suicidality of BPD. But treatment exists, has great evidence, and works better than medications for almost all conditions. It's called therapy and comes In a few different varieties that work.

Our best-known sensitive male teen fearing a life alone, Romeo, nailed it while looking at the sleeping Juliette:

For fear of that, I still will stay with thee,

And never from this palace of dim night

Depart again. Here, here will I remain

With worms that are thy chamber maids. Oh, here Will I set up my everlasting rest,

And shake the yoke of inauspicious stars

From this world-wearied flesh. Eyes, look your last.

Arms, take your last embrace. And, lips, O you

The doors of breath, seal with a righteous kiss

A dateless bargain to engrossing death."

This wasn't ignored in the Globe Theater in the 1700s. Let's catch up to our ancestors in recognizing tragedy. BPD kills people. Our silence makes us complicit; let's cut that out.
